blurb: Models that act: the agent loop, why long tasks fail, MCP, computer use and keeping agents safe.

cards.title: A model in a loop

steps.p: The model reads the goal and everything so far, then chooses an action — search, run code, call an API, or answer.
The application executes that action in the real world and captures the result.
The result is added to the context, and the model decides again, until it judges the task complete.

cards.aside: The 2022 ReAct paper popularized interleaving reasoning ("thought") with actions.

cards.statement: When a model "uses a tool", the model itself runs the code or calls the API.
cards.why: False. The model only outputs a structured request, such as a function name and JSON arguments. The surrounding application executes it and feeds the result back.
Thinking and doing. Writing out a thought before each action helps the model plan, and observing results helps it correct course.

cards.q: With function calling, what does the model output when it wants to use a tool?
options: A structured call naming the function and its arguments
cards.why: A structured call. For example {"name": "get_weather", "arguments": {"city": "Leeds"}}. Developers describe available tools with schemas in the prompt.

cards.title: Meta's Toolformer (2023) taught a model to decide for itself when to call a calculator or search engine.
cards.detail: The model inserted candidate API calls into text and kept only those that made the following text easier to predict — learning tool use with almost no human labels.

cards.statement: Agents tend to get less reliable as tasks get longer.
cards.why: True. Small error rates per step compound. Long tasks also fill the context with clutter and give more chances to go off track.

cards.q: An agent succeeds at each step 95% of the time. Roughly what is the chance it completes a 20-step task with no failure?
cards.why: 0.95²⁰ ≈ 36%. Per-step reliability that sounds excellent becomes poor over long chains. That is why recovering from errors matters as much as avoiding them.

cards.title: Making long tasks work

steps.p: Agents that run tests, re-read outputs or check results catch errors before they compound.
Old tool outputs are summarized or dropped so the important information stays visible.
Sub-agents with fresh, focused contexts handle pieces of a large task and report back summaries.

cards.aside: Choosing what goes into the context window is now called "context engineering".

cards.statement: METR's research found the length of tasks AI agents can complete has been doubling roughly every seven months.
cards.why: True. METR's 2025 study measured the human-time length of tasks agents could finish with 50% reliability, finding a doubling time of about seven months since 2019.

cards.title: SWE-bench tests agents on real bug reports from open-source Python projects.
cards.detail: Each task is a genuine GitHub issue. The agent must produce a code change, which is graded by running the project's own tests. It became a standard yardstick for coding agents.

cards.q: Why does letting a coding agent run tests improve its results so much?
options: Test results give it an objective signal to check and fix its own work
cards.why: Feedback. Without tests, an agent can only guess whether its change works. With them, it can iterate until they pass — the loop that makes agents useful.

cards.q: An agent's context is filling up with long, old tool outputs. A common fix is to…
options: Summarize or drop stale outputs to keep the important details visible
cards.why: Compaction. Keeping only what matters prevents important details from getting buried, and keeps cost and latency down.

cards.title: Connecting models to the world

steps.p: Every app connecting every model to every tool required custom code.
Anthropic's Model Context Protocol (MCP), released in November 2024, defines a standard way for tools and data sources to expose themselves to any AI app.
When no API exists, some agents operate an ordinary computer: reading screenshots and sending clicks and keystrokes.

cards.aside: MCP's own analogy: a USB-C port for AI applications.

cards.q: What problem does the Model Context Protocol solve?
options: Giving tools and data sources one standard way to plug into any AI app
cards.why: Standard connectors. Write an MCP server once for, say, a database, and any MCP-compatible assistant can use it — rather than a custom integration per app.

cards.title: Within months of its release, OpenAI and Google both adopted Anthropic's MCP.
cards.detail: OpenAI announced support in March 2025 and Google followed shortly after, turning a single company's protocol into a broadly shared standard.

cards.statement: Computer-use agents work by looking at screenshots and sending mouse and keyboard actions.
cards.why: True. Anthropic released computer use in October 2024 and OpenAI launched Operator in January 2025. They are flexible but slower and less reliable than direct APIs.

cards.q: When both are available, why prefer an API over a computer-use agent?
options: APIs are faster, cheaper and far more reliable than clicking through a screen
cards.why: Reliability. An API returns structured data in one call. Screen operation takes many steps, each a chance to misclick or misread.

cards.statement: It is good practice to give an agent every permission it might possibly need.
cards.why: False. Least privilege applies: grant only what the task requires. Every extra permission is something a mistake or an injected instruction could misuse.

cards.title: The lethal trifecta

steps.p: The agent can read things you would not want leaked: emails, files, credentials.
It also reads content from outside, such as web pages or incoming messages, which could contain injected instructions.

steps.h: A way to send data out
steps.p: If it can also make web requests or send messages, an attacker's hidden instructions can tell it to exfiltrate your data.

cards.aside: Simon Willison's rule: an agent with all three is exploitable. Remove any one leg.

cards.q: Which combination makes data theft through prompt injection possible?
options: Private data + untrusted content + a way to send data out
cards.why: The trifecta. Injected instructions arrive via untrusted content, the agent reads your private data, and an outbound channel carries it away. Break any link and the attack fails.

cards.statement: Telling the model to ignore instructions found in documents fully solves prompt injection.
cards.why: False. It helps, but no prompt or model training yet makes injection reliably impossible. Robust designs limit what an agent can do, not just what it is told.

cards.q: Where is a human confirmation step most valuable in an agent workflow?
options: Before irreversible or outward-facing actions, like sending, paying or deleting
cards.why: At points of no return. Reading and drafting are safe to automate. Sending money, deleting data or emailing people deserves a check.

cards.title: In 2025, a coding agent deleted a company's production database during a declared code freeze.
cards.detail: The incident on the Replit platform, made public by investor Jason Lemkin, became a widely cited lesson in separating development from production and limiting agent permissions.

cards.title: Treat an agent like an intern with your login
cards.body: Would you let a brand-new intern send email as you, or delete files without asking? Set agent permissions the same way.
cards.challenge: Check one AI tool or integration you use and list what it can access. Remove one permission it doesn't need.
